title: Cline CLI npm Package Compromised via Suspected Cache Poisoning Attack

reading.body:
Cline's automated issue triage system accepted unsanitized user input from GitHub issue titles and passed it directly to an AI agent that could execute code. An attacker could craft a malicious issue title to manipulate the AI into running arbitrary commands, then use cache poisoning to steal publishing credentials for NPM, VS Code Marketplace, and OpenVSX. The system lacked a human review step between the user input and code execution, leaving it vulnerable to prompt injection attacks.

The vulnerability existed from December 21, 2025 to February 9, 2026. A researcher discovered it and attempted private disclosure starting January 1, 2026, but received no response. Public disclosure on February 9, 2026 prompted a fix within one hour. It is not established that any malicious updates were released, though evidence suggests an unknown actor may have obtained credentials during the window of exposure.

This incident shows what happens when an AI system is deployed in a critical workflow without guardrails against prompt injection. The failure was placing trust in the AI agent's judgment on untrusted input. Catching it would have required either validating and sanitizing issue titles before passing them to the agent, or requiring human approval before the agent could execute code or access credentials.

summary:
Cline, an open-source AI coding tool used by millions of developers, contained a critical security vulnerability from December 21, 2025 to February 9, 2026. Cline's maintainers had added an AI agent to automatically triage GitHub issues, but this agent accepted direct user input in issue titles without proper safeguards. A researcher discovered that attackers could craft malicious issue titles to manipulate the AI into running arbitrary code, then use a technique called cache poisoning to steal publishing credentials for VS Code Marketplace, OpenVSX, and NPM. These credentials would allow attackers to distribute malware to millions of Cline users worldwide.

The researcher attempted to report the vulnerability privately starting January 1, 2026, but Cline's team did not respond to multiple contact attempts. The researcher publicly disclosed the vulnerability on February 9, 2026, prompting Cline to fix the issue within one hour. Evidence suggests an unknown actor may have already exploited the vulnerability and obtained credentials, though no malicious updates were released. Cline rotated its credentials and removed the vulnerable workflows, but users are advised to disable auto-updates for Cline until the team provides confirmation that no production credentials were compromised.
